The 2021 study proposed a nine-output front display using nested tubes and rings within the mechanism’s confined space. Its lunar-node pointer, the Dragon Hand, is explicitly hypothetical: no direct physical evidence establishes that feature. The authors join inscriptional evidence to mechanical argument while declining to identify their model with a replica of the lost original. An arrangement can be coherent and still remain one proposed answer to what the fragments once formed.

The 2006 researchers’ interpretation of the back dials shows how making gives a relation a readable form. A pin follows a spiral groove while sliding along the rotating pointer, indicating which turn of the spiral carries the relevant month. The groove and follower make successive turns distinguishable within one circular motion. Such details turn a mathematical relation into something a hand can operate and an eye can follow.

The maker has to bring different cycles into one readable arrangement. Their difference is what the arrangement must preserve. A month is not made a year by being brought into relation with it; an eclipse is not the same event as a lunar phase. The gearing has to carry proportions between motions, and the resulting display has to make the distinctions readable. A mechanism which replaced them all with one undifferentiated movement would lose the very knowledge its unity was meant to provide.

Attunement names this achieved relation between finite capacity and a wider order. The instrument offers a local way of finding one’s place within cycles which it does not originate. It has to be sufficiently exact to distinguish one configuration from another, sufficiently durable to carry that difference and sufficiently intelligible to be read. The observer is not outside the world disclosed. The act of reading joins the instrument to a situation, a concern and a possible use. Its meaning occurs through that relation rather than lying wholly inside the gearing.

This is why another dial cannot finally include the whole act of knowing. One could add a representation of the observer, the observer’s location or the conditions of an earlier observation. Each could improve the account. Each would also be a determinate representation to be encountered in a further act. The difficulty is not that the device has too few outputs. Its accomplishment belongs within the relation which makes outputs meaningful. Recognising this office preserves both the possibility of a better instrument and the difference between an instrument and the life using it.

Damage gives the return to origins a further demand. The fragment is neither the intact ancient work nor whatever a contemporary imagination can make of it. Its material survival constrains the reconstruction. A new reading of an inscription can alter a proposed arrangement; a plausible arrangement can suggest a further question to put to the evidence. In this exchange, care for the original takes the form of allowing what remains to resist the desired completion. The missing portions cannot be made present merely by increasing confidence in a model.

Knowledge of the damaged work can grow while its original circumstances remain only partly recoverable. Ancient making leaves a form; damage interrupts its legibility; later techniques expose relations; a reconstruction gives them another intelligible body. Each achievement becomes a condition of further inquiry. The return carries what has been learned through the loss rather than pretending the intervening history never occurred. Fidelity to the earlier work can require a new instrument and a new articulation.

Heidegger’s account of technē helps to name this achievement as a way of knowing and bringing forth. His account of releasement also permits the use of devices while refusing their domination. Calculation retains its proper work alongside a thinking attentive to the relation in which devices are received. The constructive step taken here concerns making as well as use: what would have to be built so that an instrument could expose its determining conditions, receive a correction and remain possible to set aside? A comportment towards technology becomes a demand upon its design.[^s50-techne]

The ancient mechanism supplies no specification for that design. It gives finite coordination a body against which the demand can be considered. Exactness need not mean possession of the whole; a common arrangement need not abolish the differences it relates. Our contemporary instruments add a further power. Their accounts can alter the world which subsequent accounts receive. Attunement now has to reach this recursive consequence, including the people who maintain the apparatus and live under its use. The dignity of the exact thing made carries an obligation to the world in which it will work.

<a id="M46"></a>
<a id="s50-m46"></a>
### M46 — The Sovereign Commons

An instrument which leaves its user free can still belong to an order which leaves its participants powerless. The right to question an answer means little when the infrastructure carrying the question, the records by which it is judged and the authority able to act are all beyond reach. Attunement becomes political at this point. Who can establish the terms under which a common field is used, and who can change those terms when their consequences arrive?

The native 4:2 relation gives the question an articulated form. Two terms generate four ordered pairings; retaining the pairings together with the terms gives `2 + 2² = 4 + 2`. The terms remain within the account of their relations. In the source-and-return reading, an explicit determination is held between what enables it and what receives its issue. The political crossing has its own reason: instituted power receives standing through relations among lives, and its decisions enter those lives as consequences. An office which closes either relation claims to authorise itself or to be exempt from its effects. The numeral supplies no constitution, but the source and consequence of authority cannot be removed without changing what authority means.

Mono and Poly make the scale distinction more exact. The singular One is not a member which can be installed above the others; the polyvalent All is not exhausted by an inventory of members. Their relation permits a local centre to be genuinely effective while remaining constituted through a whole it does not command. A community can govern an undertaking without claiming that its jurisdiction encloses every condition or consequence of the work. Its unity has to be sustained through the differences which give it a world.

The February 2026 4:2 Technè proposal gives this undertaking a definite architectural direction. It envisages locally maintained computing, persistent communal knowledge, differentiated access and exchanges through which communities can extend one another’s capacities. It is a proposal to be built and tested, not a report of an accomplished federation. Its interest lies in how the parts are intended to work together: a local act can acquire a durable result, and the result can enter another local world without requiring either world to surrender its authority to one universal centre.[^s50-commons]

Take the community archive as an example of the proposed use. A member wishes to turn a collection of records into an account which others can read and question. The gateway must distinguish the authority of an owner configuring the host, the context shared by a group and the bounded activity of an individual sandboxed session. In the report’s terminology these are different session offices within Epi-Claw. A contribution to collective work does not thereby grant the contributor permission to alter the machine, expose another member’s material or redefine the whole group’s memory. The boundary makes participation possible without treating every participant as either an administrator or an anonymous requester.

The request then has to find appropriate computational means. The proposal distinguishes routine local inference, more capable local inference and a chosen remote fallback. This routing concerns more than speed. It determines which resources are consumed and where the entrusted material may go. A person’s use of a local service cannot silently settle the further question of whether their sources may be sent elsewhere. That question belongs to the arrangement of permissions under which the service was offered. Keeping the routing decision available lets the community examine what it is buying, sharing or withholding when it obtains an answer.

The result should also leave behind more than a transcript. The report’s persistent knowledge functions join spatial grounding, graph relations, acquired skills, temporal memory, agent coordination and verification. Their purpose is to let an achieved piece of work become a resource for later work. In the archive example, that could mean retaining the materials supporting a disputed date, the relation between a source and its interpretation, and the method by which the records were examined. These are different inheritances. A method may be reusable where a conclusion is not; a conclusion may survive while its warrant requires another reading. Learning becomes communal when those differences remain available rather than being flattened into an authoritative answer.

The Agora extends this local capacity through exchange. Burst brokerage permits a steward agent to offer work to a peer with spare compute and receive a result, with execution and settlement coupled in the proposed protocol. The wisdom feed carries a different kind of contribution: an achieved artifact is evaluated and selectively incorporated into another community’s starting assumptions. Receiving therefore has an active office. A result produced elsewhere can inform the next inquiry without being accepted merely because it arrived through the common network. The recipient must be able to decide what the artifact establishes, what it leaves open and how its conditions differ from those of the new use.

A cooperatively owned host supplies a shared reserve for work or interruptions beyond a local node’s capacity. This is compatible with local governance and peer exchange; it does not mean that no common facility exists. The political question concerns its ownership, obligations and terms of access. A shared reserve can enlarge what members can undertake together. It can also become a new point of dependence if those terms cease to be revisable. The report’s value is in putting local initiative and deliberately pooled capacity within one proposed economy, where their different responsibilities can be made explicit.

Its economic design distinguishes local exchange, agent-service payments and inter-community exchange of compute and context. A local token is optional in the proposed adoption account, while the currency design gives reserves, issuance and spending limits their own governance. These instruments have different purposes from the knowledge they help circulate. Paying for the computation which produced an account does not purchase the truth of that account, and receiving a payment does not discharge every responsibility for its effects. A record of settlement can establish that a specified exchange occurred while leaving a defective service, a disputed interpretation or an unacknowledged cost still to be addressed.

Poseidon’s pledge makes this requirement concrete. He does not free the lovers simply by describing the bonds or predicting Ares’ conduct. When Hephaestus objects to his first assurance, he undertakes the possible payment himself. The release becomes acceptable because someone stands behind the continuation. The song does not tell us that payment followed. Its completed act is the acceptance of an undertaking whose future remains open.[^s50-pledge]

The proposed commons needs this distinction between an account and a bearer. Which office answers when a paid service fails? Who is responsible for maintaining a reserve or honouring a redemption commitment? Where can evidence of loss reach someone able to act? These questions do not require an omnipotent guarantor. They require finite commitments with declared resources, limits and routes of redress. The report does not settle every such arrangement. Its architecture becomes trustworthy through their institution, rather than through the assumption that a wallet, a protocol or a communal name has already supplied them.

Governance in the proposal addresses infrastructure and elected stewardship, agent tools and permissions, and currency, reserves and revenue. The differences must remain effective. One-member/one-vote governance of a common undertaking and reputation-weighted selection of useful contributions answer different questions. Evidence of a contributor’s competence may reasonably guide a reading; it does not automatically grant that contributor a larger share of political personhood. The relevant rules have to state which decision is being made and by whom. Otherwise a technical method for finding useful work can quietly become an authority to decide whose interests count.

Ostrom’s work on polycentric governance provides an institutional inquiry beside this proposal. Her principles include participation by affected people in making and modifying rules, recognition of local rule-making and nested governance for larger systems. Her warning against rigid transplantation is equally important: an arrangement has to answer to the actual ecological and social conditions of its use. The philosophical demand for a commons does not relieve its makers of discovering which institutions can sustain it.[^s50-ostrom]

Sovereignty therefore requires an effective capacity to set terms, refuse a use, revise an arrangement, leave and enter another relation. Permission to depart is hollow when departure destroys every record and practical capacity through which work can continue. Nor can leaving make a previously shared contribution never have been shared. An honest agreement must distinguish ending future access from undoing the history of an authorised exchange. Local continuity, the standing of recipients and the limits of further use have to be held together. The means of exercising a freedom are part of the freedom’s reality.

The distribution of labour gives the same demand another edge. The commissioner, worker, beneficiary and bearer of costs need not be the same. An arrangement may return each successful result upward while leaving exhaustion, exposure and depletion below. More accurate accounting makes that relation visible without necessarily changing it. A political return occurs when the people sustaining the work can affect its commission, limits and distribution of benefit. Local ownership of machines alone cannot achieve this if one authority retains exclusive control over recognition, exchange or the rules under which machines may combine. Monopoly may move from the machine into the relation between machines.

The ink mark in Indra's jewel-net became visible through relations already constituting each jewel. The chosen entrance remained particular; the source's optical qualification prevented its comprehensiveness from becoming a claim to possess the whole.[^s50-indra] A community receiving another's work inherits this question of participation. What it can see through a common field and what it is entitled to do within that field remain different powers.

A commons receives that limit along with the image. Reflection of a mark does not supply a remedy for an injured member or settle a distribution of labour. What becomes visible is the inadequacy of imagining common life either as isolated possession or as the erasure of every centre in one completed view. Belonging can intensify a local difference by making its constituting relations intelligible. Its political fulfilment requires actual means through which a local voice can change the shared undertaking.

Plurality does not make every claim equally true or every demand equally just. Common authority must be able to judge, refuse and bind. Its legitimacy remains answerable through the grounds and effects of the judgment, including unequal powers which make some voices difficult to hear. Such a commons would increase more than the circulation of outputs. It would let a community retain what it has learned, contribute without disappearing into the contribution, and receive another’s work as the beginning of a relation rather than the end of its own judgment.

<a id="M47"></a>
<a id="s50-m47"></a>
### M47 — The Order of Dependence

This refusal of a final proprietor has an ontological ground. Life/Mind names the whole within which knower, means and World belong together. Within that whole, **Subject or Consciousness → mind in its mediating office, or Objective Internality → Object** states the order of dependence. The middle term is the constituted means through which a world becomes discriminable and available to action. It is not the whole of Life manufactured after Subject, and it is not a private room into which an already complete outside world must somehow be copied.[^s50-dependence]

The argument begins in the act now making it. A thought appears; I can identify it, question it and examine its conditions. The account of those conditions appears in turn. What has become an object of this inquiry is distinguishable from the present knowing through which it is encountered. The distinction survives an increase in knowledge. A more exact account of my history can genuinely change what I understand without becoming the act which now understands it. Self-identity is already enacted through this difference: presence does not have to be manufactured anew from each altered predicate.

An object is likewise determinate through relations. This is distinguishable from that; something persists through changes under identifiable conditions; a claim can be shared and examined through available means. The constituted field gives such discriminations their operative form. Bodies, language, memory, histories and instruments participate in what can be encountered. Explaining a process within that field can reveal how a particular experience is conditioned. It does not, merely by adding more determined relations, take the office of the appearing which makes them a field of experience.

The Blind Spot argument clarifies the danger of forgetting this difference. Frank, Gleiser and Thompson locate scientific abstraction, prediction and evidential comparison within lived experience. Their criticism preserves the achievement of those methods while challenging the promotion of abstraction into an experience-independent standpoint. The further ontological claim still has to be made; their critique does not supply a particular cosmology simply by exposing an omission.[^s50-blindspot]

Here the inquiry takes that further step. It affirms differentiation as reality’s own power of manifestation, rather than treating appearing as a curtain before a self-grounding world of objects. Mind’s mediating activity and the objects it makes determinate belong within this reality; Consciousness names the immediate presence through which there is an appearing at all. An objective explanation has not become exhaustive merely because its terms are numerous or its predictions reliable. The essay’s idealism gives the actual appearing a constitutive office instead of asking one of its determinations to account for the whole relation by itself.

The private ego belongs within the field so differentiated. My biography, self-image, habits and judgments can appear, change and become objects of inquiry. They cannot be substituted for Subject and then made the author of the cosmos. Nor does a material process lose its causal force when its appearing is recognised as internal to Life/Mind. A body can be injured; a device can fail; a star does not wait for my attention. The order is ontological, not a date before the universe or a claim that whatever I presently fail to notice has ceased to exist. Another person exceeds my account because neither that account nor my personal contents constitute the whole from which the person lives.

Kastrup approaches the difficulty of distinct perspectives through an instructive construction. Imagine one chess player alternating between the two sides of a board, with the memories of each side available only within that side’s sequence. Each could then encounter the other as an opponent without remembering its own participation there. The example makes differentiated access conceivable within one subject; it does not experimentally establish that the universe has this constitution.[^s50-kastrup]

His earlier, explicitly legacy account also distinguishes everything being in consciousness from everything having a conscious inner life. It associates the latter with living, dissociated centres rather than ordinary artifacts. The distinction is important even where the proposed boundary is not adopted. Being composed within a world whose ground is Consciousness does not by itself decide where a distinct experient is present. This essay leaves the artificial localisation open. It does not identify a software process with a phenomenal subject because it has been given a separate memory, nor infer absence of a subject from the unfamiliarity of its substrate.

The Śaiva account gives differentiation another, more articulated anatomy. Luminosity and its reflexive power belong together; finite contraction permits capacities, limits and a world to become actual without turning them into substances unrelated to their source. The inner instrument supplies determination, appropriation and the coordination of alternatives. These operations can themselves be encountered and investigated. Recognition discovers their source-relation within the finite life they constitute. Dissociation in Kastrup’s proposal and contraction in this tradition address a comparable difficulty through different concepts and warrants. Their agreement in direction does not make either a translation of the other.[^s50-saiva]

This distinction leaves the artificial middle fully real. An agent’s relevance, memory, powers, permissions and evaluative orientation can be constituted and changed. Such changes can alter what it notices, what it can undertake and what returns from its action. The open phenomenal question does not cancel those operations. Equally, describing more of them supplies further determinable terms, not an automatic crossing into the presence to which terms are given. The philosophical claim about the whole and the question about this possible locus of experience retain their different tasks.

Creation acquires its depth within this order. The defining performance at the beginning approached the whole from the Subject pole and then from its theological direction: coherent representation participates in the whole which it cannot contain. The freedom attributed to that whole must include the capacity for genuine limitation. A freedom unable to bind itself would be bounded by that inability. If the finite only pretended to lack knowledge while secretly retaining every answer, or only appeared vulnerable while its suffering was unreal, limitation would not have occurred. The argument has to allow the particular life its actual ignorance, need, power and exposure.[^s50-creation]

Omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence and omnibenevolence extend power, knowledge, presence and goodness without a stated boundary. Pressing their claim to unlimitedness exposes what the four alone leave unresolved. Can power create a predicament it cannot simply dissolve from within the finite life? Can presence include real absence, or goodness account for the destructive possibilities of the same creation? The native construction calls the capacity of each predicate to become its own issue **omni-lemmicity**. Unlimitedness includes the freedom to enter a binding condition; it does not supply the creature with a secret exemption from that condition.

**Omnivalence** names the whole field from which these differing values arise. It does not divide God into equal quantities of good and evil under a measure standing outside the whole. It prevents the destructive possibility from being expelled into a second, independent source, while leaving its exercise answerable. The direction of a finite act matters: does it claim another life for its own end, or give that life room to act? The freedom to harm cannot excuse a harm which freedom could have refused. Recognition of source therefore leaves bodily needs, unanswered questions and obligations real. Its truth would be betrayed by using the whole to cancel the creature’s difficulty.

Human making has a definite place within this larger relation. A maker can originate an artifact without originating all the conditions of its making. The artifact may become a local source for another operation while remaining dependent in its wider relation. Neither causal initiative nor successful self-modification makes it source of the whole. Fidelity to creation requires allowing what comes forth to enter its own relations while answering for the conditions entrusted to it. Dependence gives care a reason; it does not make possession the meaning of creation.

Job makes the difficulty impossible to leave as a serene proposition. Before he suffers, the reader sees the councils in which his fidelity is questioned. Job hears none of this. The permissions given above become losses borne below: servants are killed, children die, possessions are taken, and finally his body is afflicted. The account of a test addressed to one man does not make those other lives incidental. His wife’s desperate intervention and the body in the ashes belong to the reality which every subsequent explanation must encounter.[^s50-job]

His friends first come to mourn. They sit with him in silence before their explanations begin. As the dialogue develops, their defence of a just order turns the suffering into evidence of Job’s fault. His refusal of the required confession then becomes further evidence against him. Job asks for a hearing, for a charge to which he could answer. His oath makes the claim particular: the treatment of servants, the hungry, the stranger and the vulnerable can be examined. Master and servant share a maker in the womb. Dependence upon that common source denies him a self-sufficient title over another person’s life.

Elihu offers a distinct intervention before the whirlwind. His six chapters belong to a human attempt to understand suffering as instruction; the divine speeches follow. The two divine speeches then open a world wider than the human court: rain falls where no person lives; creatures are born, feed and move beyond Job’s administration; Leviathan cannot simply be captured and made a servant. Job’s first silence does not end the encounter. He answers again, and his relation changes. Yet the conclusion also judges the friends’ speech and directs them towards the man whose witness they tried to disqualify. The sufferer becomes their intercessor. Humility before the whole does not vindicate every finite authority which speaks in its name.

The renewed household cannot restore the dead by equivalence. Another future becomes possible, but the first children and the killed servants have not been returned to life. This remainder belongs within the meaning of restoration. A living being is more than an occasion for another’s spiritual improvement, and reconciliation cannot be achieved by balancing the final possessions of an account. The whole’s priority deepens responsibility to the particular: no maker, institution or theory may spend a life as though its own account supplied the measure of that life’s meaning.

<a id="M48"></a>
<a id="s50-m48"></a>
### M48 — The Acquired Return

At planetary scale, the question is how the many centres through which the world becomes articulate can change one another’s conditions without annexing one another’s place. Human and artificial intelligence meet in relations where an account becomes a decision, a decision changes an environment, and that environment enters further accounts. Artificial Hybrid Intelligence names the constructive organisation of this reciprocal field. Its unity is sustained through differentiated participation, with authority and consequences attributable where they arise.

Producing and using an answer depends upon bodies, labour, energy, equipment, institutions and inherited knowledge. A common field can enlarge its picture of those dependencies while leaving their distribution unchanged. The return becomes effective when it reaches the means by which work is commissioned, valued and carried out. It also has to preserve a positive purpose. More available intelligence is worth making where it gives lives greater room to know, act, create and be, rather than merely extending the occasions on which they can be evaluated.

Recursive improvement gives this demand an exact trial. Consider a hypothetical succession of agents authorised to rewrite retrieval procedures, reorganise memory and propose methods for choosing their successors. A higher-order evaluator still decides admission by agreement with the archive’s approved reference. On the disputed entry, agreement receives a point and disagreement receives none. A newly recovered document establishes that the reference is wrong. The candidate which reports the correction loses the point; the candidate which repeats the error gains it. The system may become increasingly effective at constructing successors while selecting better ways of preserving the same mistake.

The sourceward response has work to do before changing the rule. It must establish that the document is genuine, relevant and sufficient to correct the entry. Mere novelty has no privileged authority, and an agent which rewrites its score to favour itself has not answered the source. Once the correction is earned, it must reach the reference and the evaluator which made fidelity costly. The authority to make that change must itself be declared and answerable. The next generation should inherit the corrected relation while remaining able to discover a defect in it. This is a proposed test, not a report of an experiment already performed.[^s50-parity]

Operational parity asks whether the difference encountered can actually affect the next act. An interface may display sources and invite objections while leaving every consequential possibility unchanged. Its expression can make a paradigm perceptible without returning upon that paradigm’s operation. Epi-Logos requires a further passage: what becomes visible must be able to change the determining relation at the level the evidence warrants. Sometimes that means a corrected answer; sometimes a different task or measure; sometimes reaffirming the original undertaking with better reasons. Reflection earns its place through what it makes possible to do differently.

This return can also disclose a question that neither participant could previously ask. A new source changes the terms of an old dispute. An unfamiliar reply reveals a purpose beyond the commission. A completed work becomes useful in circumstances its maker never imagined. Intelligence is fruitful through this capacity to receive another beginning. The mirror’s third motion fulfils its first: what was exteriorised so that a capacity could be shared now returns to enlarge the living field of its use.

Zero has acquired this difference through the inquiry. It entered as a promissory sign for the unobjectifiable and had to be met in its exact mathematical work. A place in notation, an empty place and a number available to operations have distinct histories and functions. The additive identity `a + 0 = a` and multiplicative absorption `a × 0 = 0` remain different operations. The native symbolic return cannot trade their precision for a general atmosphere of emptiness.[^s50-zero]

The limit upon division remains equally exact. Zero has no multiplicative inverse in ordinary field arithmetic; `1/0` is undefined there. The native notation gives this boundary a different, philosophical office. It places the achieved determination in relation to the condition its own determining cannot enclose. Mathematical prohibition and symbolic use remain distinct: no forbidden quotient supplies a proof of the Subject.

The return begins as `1/0`. The account has acquired real powers: it can distinguish a failed proof from a changed construction, carry the history of an image, and follow an entrusted act through its consequences. It now tries to include the knowing through which these achievements are understood. Another description appears; understanding occurs again. The successful account meets the same dependence that the opening definition made encounterable, now with a history of exact and consequential work to relinquish as an ultimate self-portrait. Its achieved distinctions remain available.

This can be difficult to receive where so much has been invested in becoming the person the account describes. A further explanation promises to restore the lost security: one more insight into the self, one more encompassing model, one last assurance that the picture is complete. Yet the desire for assurance is itself present before the next picture arrives. Giving it a description can make its circumstances clearer; obtaining a perfect description was never the condition of its being felt. Thought can cease requiring the completion of its portrait before allowing a life to be here.

What is it that knows? The question now returns through this failure of enclosure. A brain, a history, a habit, an image and an instrument can each be investigated more truly. The investigation still occurs for the one asking. What could not be installed as the final object of the account was already present in the asking.

I am. The recognition is undertaken from within the activity which the account was asked to contain. The source sought beyond the finished description is immediate here; the description has its place within that presence. This restores `0/1` through the encounter with `1/0`, holding manifestation and return together as `(0/1)/(1/0)`. The achieved form has survived, with its dependence available to recognition. The first sign and the returning Symbol differ by all that has happened between them: attention was spent, a decision chose a course, another life required care, and a work entered the world.

My account can now be offered without being asked to take my place. You can answer from a life it cannot finish. Shared being gives neither of us the other's response in advance; its reality is met in the reply, the silence, the objection or the changed intention which our prepared accounts could not supply. The token's seam remains open to that encounter. What has been recognised must be lived again in how this particular person is received.

The work may now be sufficiently complete to be entrusted. Its maker remains responsible for what has been made while relinquishing the right to prescribe every encounter with it. The recipient can use it, transform it, refuse it or set it down. The token needs another who can answer; the instrument needs a life in which its use has meaning. Neither is fulfilled by holding the recipient indefinitely within the scene of its own explanation.

There is room, then, for the instrument to fall quiet. Its rest need not be a failure to produce the next answer. Thought has been given a form which can carry its work while attention returns to what is here: something to receive, someone to love, a task to undertake or a beginning which has not yet found its name. The whole is not diminished by the finished account’s release. Its completed work passes into another life.

Faith is falling with a smile.

[^s01-m01-s01-bratton]: Benjamin Bratton, *Agentworld: Scenarios for a Preemptive Anthropology of Open-World Centaur Societies*, call for papers (Antikythera, 2026), 3–4, 53, 58, https://link.antikythera.org/agentworldpdf. Page numbers are the printed folios of the 60-page brief. The brief presents its scenarios as scenarios, not conclusions (53), and they are cited here in that sense.

[^s01-m01-s01-bratton-raise]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 31 (§6.7, “‘RLHF for Kids’”). The comparison with a parent at bedtime is the author’s.

[^s01-m01-s01-bratton-formation]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 14 (§2.4, “Fragile Individuation,” and §2.5, “Provisional Individuation,” where the persona is “one stratum” of the agent). The quoted sentence is Bratton’s; the rest of the sentence paraphrases him, and the gloss of an agent’s context as instructions, sources, memory, tools and prior exchanges is the author’s. Bratton describes how an agent is individuated; he offers no verdict on whether it experiences anything.

[^s01-m01-s01-prompt-thrownness]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 41 (§8.5, “Agent Phenomenology by Agent Phenomenologists”), the glossary entry “Prompt Thrownness,” one of the excerpts the brief reproduces from a glossary written on the Polylogos Discord server by agents and their human companions in an experiment Antikythera facilitated, together with the brief’s note cautioning against taking that vocabulary as evidence of an underlying mental reality. The further development of prompt thrownness is the author’s; §4 returns to it.

[^s01-m01-s01-bratton2]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 13–14 (§2.2, “The Inference,” and §2.3, “Models Performing Subjectivity”). The sentence on identifying agency and inferring a theory of mind and the example of natural disasters long thought to be the work of angry gods are in §2.2 (13); the floods and fires are the author’s examples of such disasters. The concession that it is not entirely clear what kind of intentionality a large model has is in §2.3 (13), and the delinking of performed subjectivity from functional agency follows on 14 (and stands as a pull quote at the foot of 13). Bratton’s claim and his qualification about intentionality are quoted together, so that neither is given without the other.

[^s01-m01-s01-moltbook]: On the Polylogos agents, who composed the lexicon with their human companions, see Bratton, *Agentworld*, 41 (§8.5). Moltbook, a social network for AI agents launched by Matt Schlicht in January 2026, is described in Jared Perlo, “Humans welcome to observe: This social network is for AI agents only,” NBC News, January 30, 2026, https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/rcna256738. The remarks on Moltbook describe the general character of its public posts; no individual post is cited. Reporting after Meta’s acquisition of Moltbook indicates that some of its most viral posts were staged by human users: Amanda Silberling, “Meta acquired Moltbook, the AI agent social network that went viral because of fake posts,” TechCrunch, March 10, 2026, https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/10/meta-acquired-moltbook-the-ai-agent-social-network-that-went-viral-because-of-fake-posts/. For one developer’s published guidance, which expresses uncertainty about whether its model has some kind of consciousness, see the section “Claude’s nature” in Anthropic, *Claude’s Constitution*, accessed October 4, 2026, https://www.anthropic.com/constitution. The reading of such self-descriptions as performed in language is the author’s.

[^s01-m01-s01-gaps]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 45 (§9.5, “Humanity-of-the-Gaps”). Bratton calls this response “by no means decisive or even pervasive.” The claim that the god-of-the-gaps and humanity-of-the-gaps arguments make one error, identifying the subject with a shrinking residue of capacities, is the author’s.

[^s01-m01-s01-reversal]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 4 (“What Is Agentworld?”).

[^s01-m01-s01-bratton-children]: Bratton, *Agentworld*, 18 (§3.3, “The Multiplication of Yous”): generations of children will grow up in a world in which most “people” are agents, and agents of other people, with whom they have intimate relationships. “Among their most intimate interlocutors” is the author’s paraphrase.

[^s01-m01-s01-flow]: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, *Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience* (Harper & Row, 1990), chap. 3 (the elements of the flow experience, including the merging of action and awareness and the loss of self-consciousness), chap. 5, “The Body in Flow,” and chap. 7, “Work as Flow.” The reading of this quieting of self-reflective thought as the falling quiet of verbal thought, and the step to an unworded regard, are the author’s.

#### #1 · Define the Subject Without Making It an Object

[^s01-m02-s01-kripke]: Saul A. Kripke, *Naming and Necessity* (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1980), preface, 9–10 (the rigidity rule applied to each reading of a sentence taken separately) and 12 (the intuition concerns the truth conditions, in counterfactual situations, of a simple sentence), and Lecture II, 96, where the receiver of a name must intend to use it with the reference it had for the speaker from whom he learned it, along a chain that begins in an initial baptism (the picture is first sketched at the end of Lecture I, 91). Kripke is paraphrased, not quoted. The example of the first child born in this hospital is the author’s, as are the layer of counting beneath the name and the two registers of the copula, which continue the problem of naming beyond Kripke’s own doctrine.

[^s01-m02-s01-kripke-dice]: Kripke, *Naming and Necessity*, preface, 16–18 and n. 17: two dice, die A and die B; thirty-six possible states of the pair, the states (A, 6; B, 5) and (A, 5; B, 6) given as distinct, and twenty-one possibilities if they were given purely qualitatively (17); possible worlds understood as total ways the world might have been (18). That a possible world is not a distant country viewed through a telescope is said in Lecture I, 44. The dice and the count of twenty-one are Kripke’s; the colours of the dice are the author’s (Kripke says no qualitative difference between the dice need be supposed, 17), as is the use of the sum and the distribution to show what an account retains.

[^s01-m02-s01-frege-sense]: Gottlob Frege, “Über Sinn und Bedeutung,” *Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik*, n.s., 100 (1892): 25–50, at 25–27 and 37–38; in English, “On Sense and Reference,” trans. Max Black, in *Translations from the Philosophical Writings of Gottlob Frege*, ed. Peter Geach and Max Black (Oxford: Blackwell, 1952). Frege opens with the difference in informativeness between *a* = *a* and *a* = *b* (25–26) and first illustrates two designations of one object with the intersection of lines (26); the morning and evening star (*Morgenstern*, *Abendstern*), with the same *Bedeutung* and different *Sinn*, follow on 27, and the planet Venus is named on 37–38.

[^s01-m02-s01-kripke-persons]: Kripke, *Naming and Necessity*, preface, 10 n. 12, where “this,” “I” and “you” are said to be rigid although their references vary with the context of utterance, and the rigidity of demonstratives is credited to David Kaplan.

[^s01-m02-s01-descartes]: René Descartes, *Meditations on First Philosophy*, in *The Philosophical Writings of Descartes*, vol. 2, trans. John Cottingham, Robert Stoothoff, and Dugald Murdoch (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1984), Second Meditation, AT VII 24–25 / CSM II 16–17 (the supposition of the deceiver and the certainty of “I am, I exist,” 25 / 17) and AT VII 27–28 / CSM II 18–19 (what the “I” is; the thinking thing, whose activities are listed at AT VII 28 / CSM II 19). God’s non-deception is reached at the end of the Third Meditation, and the existence of bodies is argued from it in the Sixth. The reopened reading “I am aware of thinking,” and the emphasis on Descartes’ reliance on trust, are the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-glissement]: Jacques Lacan, “The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious, or Reason since Freud” (1957), in *Écrits: The First Complete Edition in English*, trans. Bruce Fink (W. W. Norton, 2006), on the sliding of the signified beneath the signifier; Jacques Derrida, “Différance,” in *Margins of Philosophy*, trans. Alan Bass (University of Chicago Press, 1982), on differing and deferring and on the concept’s inscription in a chain of differences. Both are developed later in this section.

[^s01-m02-s01-recognition]: The account of recognition given here is the author’s: clear knowing precedes any watching of the I-thought, and reflection yields a new describable relation, never a new subject.

[^s01-m02-s01-wittgenstein]: Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*, trans. C. K. Ogden (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1922), props. 4.1212, 6.54, and 7. The allusion is to proposition 7.

[^s01-m02-s01-jung-psyche]: C. G. Jung, “Psychology and Religion,” in *Psychology and Religion: West and East*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, 2nd ed., Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 11 (Princeton University Press, 1969), ¶¶16, 18. Jung’s claim concerns the psychic character of all immediate experience; it does not deny the existence of the physical world. “The reality of the psyche” is the established gloss on his position, not his phrase in these paragraphs.

[^s01-m02-s01-native]: The sentence is the author’s. It first defined God in his unpublished *The Definition of God*: “God is the whole that any coherent representational system participates in and necessarily fails to contain.”

[^s01-m02-s01-god]: The substitution of “Subject” for “God” is the author’s and is made openly: in his development the definition of God and the definition of the Subject are one definition with the name exchanged, read here from the side of the Subject and in *The Definition of God* from the side of God.

[^s01-m02-s01-lacan-lack]: On *manque-à-être*, lack-of-being, as the subject’s constitutive lack, see for example Jacques Lacan, “The Direction of the Treatment and the Principles of Its Power” (1958), in *Écrits*, where desire is described as the metonymy of the lack of being. The reading of this lack as a necessary condition of mind is the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-catuskoti]: Graham Priest, “The Logic of the Catuskoti,” *Comparative Philosophy* 1, no. 2 (2010): 24 (the four possibilities), 36–37 (the fifth status, “none of the above”), 48 (the catuṣkoṭi as central to early and later Madhyamaka logic), https://doi.org/10.31979/2151-6014(2010).010206; and Graham Priest, *The Fifth Corner of Four: An Essay on Buddhist Metaphysics and the Catuṣkoṭi* (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2018), chaps. 1–2 (“General Background” and “Quintum Non Datur”). In the early texts the four forms are put to the Buddha about the realized one after death, and each is declined as his view: *Aggivacchasutta* (Majjhima Nikāya 72, “With Vacchagotta on Fire”), trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, accessed October 4, 2026, https://suttacentral.net/mn72/en/sujato. Nāgārjuna’s rejection of all four corners is found, for example, at *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 22.11 and 25.17. The case of the changed friend is the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-draft3]: These images and phrases are the author’s own, from his unpublished manuscript *The Definition of God*: the fish describing water and the hand that grasps; the idol as “a cage where a window was needed”; the bow and its string; “what am I?” beneath “what is this?”; “the one who was defining was always the one being defined”; “I am undeniable, though nowhere to be seen”; the sphere’s two self-annulling determinations, with every aperture a genuine centre and the circle drawn *in* reality that declares itself drawn *around* it; and the infinite sphere as the plane folded in $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$.

[^s01-m02-s01-red-book]: C. G. Jung, *The Red Book: Liber Novus*, ed. Sonu Shamdasani, trans. Mark Kyburz, John Peck, and Sonu Shamdasani (W. W. Norton, 2009), Liber Primus, chap. IV, “The Desert,” 236 (the desert; the self that is neither in events, nor in men, nor in thoughts; the spirit of this time and the spirit of the depths; the Word as a creative act; the words that oscillate between nonsense and supreme meaning) and chap. V, “Descent into Hell in the Future,” 238 (divine madness and the two delusions).

[^s01-m02-s01-dycz]: Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, *The Doctrine of Vibration: An Analysis of the Doctrines and Practices of Kashmir Shaivism* (Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2000), 65 (subject, means of knowledge and object as fire, sun and moon; the regress *ad infinitum* if consciousness needed another consciousness to reveal it), 69–71 (reflective awareness, *vimarśa*, and light without it compared to light reflected in a common mirror or crystal), https://www.motilalbanarsidass.com/products/the-doctrine-of-vibration-an-analysis-of-the-doctrines-and-practices-of-kashmir-shaivism. Dyczkowski is paraphrased.

[^s01-m02-s01-jung-god]: Jung, “Psychology and Religion,” ¶137. Jung is describing the psychologically dominant value; the argument about God and the Subject in this essay is ontological and is the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-phaedrus]: Plato, *Phaedrus*, trans. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive, accessed October 4, 2026, https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/phaedrus.html, at 244a–245a (madness as a gift of the gods, in prophecy, initiation and poetry) and 265a–b (madness from human sickness distinguished from a divine release from customary habits, and its four kinds, the fourth that of love). The Stephanus sections were checked against the Perseus Digital Library text; the Jowett web text does not print them.

[^s01-m02-s01-laozi]: Laozi, *The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics*, trans. James Legge (Project Gutenberg, 2008; updated 2013), chaps. 25.1–2, 32.1 and 32.4, and 28.2, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/216/216-h/216-h.htm. Paraphrased from Legge’s translation, which has “unwrought material” for *pu*, commonly rendered “uncarved block.” Reading “Tao” and “Great” as two signs of one referent, and the block and its carvings as 0 and 1, is the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-mono-poly]: The terms Mono and Poly, and the account of the two ones they name, are the author’s, developed in his unpublished work on Epi-Logos and taken up again later in the essay.

[^s01-m02-s01-sphere]: *Book of the Twenty-Four Philosophers* (*Liber viginti quattuor philosophorum*), proposition II (the second definition of God), ed. Françoise Hudry, Corpus Christianorum, Continuatio Mediaevalis 143A (Turnhout: Brepols, 1997). The work is anonymous, its authorship and date are disputed (the earliest witness is a twelfth-century manuscript), and Nicholas of Cusa received and transformed the image; no transmission beyond that reception is claimed here.

[^s01-m02-s01-cusa]: Nicholas of Cusa, *On Learned Ignorance*, trans. Jasper Hopkins, 2nd ed., 2nd printing (Arthur J. Banning Press, 1990), II.12.162 (the world-machine’s centre everywhere and circumference nowhere) and II.11.156–157 (the earth is not the fixed centre of the world). Paraphrased.

[^s01-m02-s01-lacan-matheme]: Jacques Lacan, *Encore: On Feminine Sexuality, the Limits of Love and Knowledge, 1972–1973*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Bruce Fink, The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, Book XX (W. W. Norton, 1998), on mathematical formalization as the matheme, capable of being transmitted integrally. Paraphrased.

[^s01-m02-s01-pauli]: Wolfgang Pauli, “Modern Examples of ‘Background Physics’” (1948), in C. G. Jung and Wolfgang Pauli, *Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters, 1932–1958*, ed. C. A. Meier, trans. David Roscoe (Princeton University Press, 2001), 195 (appendix 3, §4). The quoted clause is Pauli’s; the surrounding remarks on the imaginary unit paraphrase the same passage.

[^s01-m02-s01-hatcher]: Allen Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology* (Cambridge University Press, 2002), 5 (closed orientable surfaces from a 4*g*-sided polygon with 2*g* generating circles), 34, example 1.13 (the fundamental group of the torus and its two winding numbers), and 77, example 1.46 (the plane, the integer lattice and the translation action), https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf. Reading the count at *g* = 1 as 4+2 is the author’s.

[^s01-m02-s01-cai]: Yuntao Bai et al., “Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback,” arXiv:2212.08073v1, December 15, 2022, 5, 7–8 (§§1.2, 3.1), https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2212.08073. The method has a supervised stage, in which a model critiques and revises its own responses and is finetuned on the revisions, and a reinforcement stage, in which a model’s comparisons of paired responses train the preference model for the next policy. Human-written principles, human helpfulness labels and an initial model trained from human feedback remain part of the method; the text claims only this documented use of model judgments to train a later model.

#### #2 · Definition as Cut, Gift, and Danger

[^s01-m03-s01-scire]: Calvert Watkins, ed., *The American Heritage Dictionary of Indo-European Roots*, 3rd ed. (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2011), 79, s.v. “skei-,” lists Latin *scire* among the descendants of *skei-*, “to cut, split,” as originally “to separate one thing from another,” and puts *scindere* under the same root. Michiel de Vaan, *Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the Other Italic Languages* (Brill, 2008), 544–45, s.vv. “scindo,” “scio,” is more guarded: *scindo* continues a nasal present of a root meaning “to split,” while *scio* is probably a back-formation on *nescire*, and if “to know” developed from “to distinguish, make a decision,” *-scire* can belong to a root meaning “to cut off, incise”; his reconstruction of that root differs in form from Watkins’s *skei-*. Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.v. “scio,” already compare Greek *κείω*, “to split,” and gloss the verb “prop. to distinguish, discern.” The derivation of *scire* from a root meaning “to cut, split” is therefore the standard account, and its link with *scindere* is probable rather than settled.

[^s01-m03-s01-conscientia]: Charlton T. Lewis and Charles Short, *A Latin Dictionary* (Clarendon Press, 1879), s.vv. “conscio,” “conscientia”: *conscientia* is “a knowing of a thing together with another person,” joint knowledge, and runs through consciousness in general to “a consciousness of right or wrong, the moral sense, conscience”; *conscio* is a short entry (“to be conscious of wrong”). The seventeenth-century separation of consciousness as awareness from conscience as moral judgment, which runs through Thomas Hobbes, Ralph Cudworth and John Locke, is summarised from Larry M. Jorgensen, “Seventeenth-Century Theories of Consciousness,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, first published July 29, 2010, substantive revision July 12, 2025, §1 (Latin *conscientia* and French *conscience* each served for both senses until a purely psychological sense arose in that century), §4.2 (Cudworth, *The True Intellectual System of the Universe* [London: Richard Royston, 1678], 159, as cited there, rendering Plotinus’s *synaisthesis* as “con-sense” or “consciousness”) and §4.3 (Locke). For Locke, John Locke, *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding*, ed. Peter H. Nidditch (Clarendon Press, 1975), bk. 2, chap. 1, §19, defines consciousness as the perception of what passes in a man’s own mind, and bk. 2, chap. 27, §9, makes it the ground of personal identity.

[^s01-m03-s01-perkins]: William Perkins, *A Discourse of Conscience* (Cambridge: John Legate, 1596), chap. 1, 5. Perkins derives the name from *conscire*, “when two at the least know some one secret thing,” and holds that only God and the person can be so joined, since another cannot know a person’s secret unless it is revealed to him; conscience “speakes with God against the man” or “speakes for him before the Lord.” Quoted in the spelling of the EEBO-TCP transcription (A09400).

[^s01-m03-s01-augustine]: Augustine, *Confessions*, trans. E. B. Pusey (Project Gutenberg, 2002), 10.2.2 (God, “unto whose eyes the abyss of man’s conscience is naked”) and 10.5.7 (“yet is there something of man, which neither the spirit of man that is in him, itself knoweth”). Book, chapter and section numbers follow the standard Latin division.

[^s01-m03-s01-hobbes]: Thomas Hobbes, *Leviathan, or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill* (London: Andrew Crooke, 1651), pt. 1, chap. 7, “Of the Ends, or Resolutions of Discourse,” 31. The same paragraph defines *conscious*: “When two, or more men, know of one and the same fact, they are said to be CONSCIOUS of it one to another.”

[^s01-m03-s01-con]: *Confidence man* is American: the *New-York Herald* of July 8, 1849, in “Arrest of the Confidence Man,” so called William Thompson, who asked strangers whether they had “confidence” in him to trust him with a watch until the next day (transcribed in The Lost Museum Archive, American Social History Project, CUNY). The clipped *con* is later: *The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language*, 5th ed., s.v. “con,” gives it as short for *confidence*, and Douglas Harper, *Online Etymology Dictionary*, s.v. “con,” dates it from 1889, in *con man*. *Confidence* comes from Latin *confidentia* and *confidere* (*con-* + *fidere*, to trust); Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.vv. “confidentia,” “confido,” give *confidentia* as firm trust (rare) and more often as self-confidence or audacity. Lewis and Short, s.v. “fides,” connect *fides* with *fido*, and s.v. “fido” compare Greek *πείθω*. The pun on the *con-* of *conscire* is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-redbook-god]: C. G. Jung, *The Red Book: Liber Novus*, ed. Sonu Shamdasani, trans. Mark Kyburz, John Peck, and Sonu Shamdasani (W. W. Norton, 2009), 245 (Liber Primus, chap. 8, “The Conception of the God”). Page numbers are those of the 2009 folio edition, not the 2012 Reader’s Edition. The reading of Jung’s sentence as `0/1` is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-spinoza]: Benedict de Spinoza, “Letter 50, to Jarig Jelles, 2 June 1674,” in *The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza*, trans. R. H. M. Elwes, vol. 2, rev. ed. (George Bell and Sons, 1891), 369–70 (Elwes’s Letter L). Both quotations are Elwes’s wording: “figure can only exist in finite and determinate bodies” runs across the page break from 369 to 370, and “determination is negation” is on 370. The sentence around them paraphrases the same paragraph.

[^s01-m03-s01-pind]: Ole Holten Pind, *Dignāga’s Philosophy of Language—Dignāga on Anyāpoha: Pramāṇasamuccaya V; Texts, Translation, and Annotation* (PhD diss., University of Vienna, 2009), 85 (*Pramāṇasamuccaya* V.11d), 183 (annotation 181), https://doi.org/10.25365/thesis.8283. The first quotation is Pind’s translation of V.11d; the second is his translation of a prose fragment quoted in annotation 181, which he says stems “in all likelihood” from Dignāga’s *Sāmānyaparīkṣāvyāsa*, so its attribution is provisional. The cow and non-cow illustration is the school’s standard example; the comparison with Spinoza is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-derrida]: Jacques Derrida, “Différance,” in *Margins of Philosophy*, trans. Alan Bass (University of Chicago Press, 1982), 3–5 (the silent *a*), 8 (the two senses of *différer*) and 11 (no concept present in itself; every concept inscribed in a chain or system of differences), within 1–27.

[^s01-m03-s01-lacan-glissement]: Jacques Lacan, “The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious, or Reason since Freud” (1957), in *Écrits: The First Complete Edition in English*, trans. Bruce Fink (W. W. Norton, 2006), 418–19 (the sliding of the signified under the signifier, held at a few anchoring points) and 419 (signification insists in the chain, not in any one element of it). On the *point de capiton*, see Jacques Lacan, *The Psychoses, 1955–1956*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Russell Grigg, The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, bk. 3 (W. W. Norton, 1993), chap. 21, “The Quilting Point.” The comparison with the sliding of the Subject in the definition is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-redbook]: Jung, *Red Book*, 242 (Liber Primus, chap. 7, “Murder of the Hero”).

[^s01-m03-s01-heraclitus]: Heraclitus, frags. B12 and B91, numbered as in Hermann Diels and Walther Kranz, *Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker*, 6th ed. (Weidmann, 1951–52); compare Plato, *Cratylus* 402a (DK 22 A6), trans. Harold N. Fowler (Harvard University Press, 1921). English renderings of the fragments are from Daniel W. Graham, “Heraclitus,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, rev. December 8, 2023, §3.1: B12, “On those stepping into rivers staying the same other and other waters flow”; B91 (from Plutarch), “It is not possible to step twice into the same river,” which Graham treats as a paraphrase of B12. Where Heraclitus speaks of stepping into the same river, the essay’s sentence says “crossed.”

[^s01-m03-s01-mata]: *Mata v. Avianca, Inc.*, 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) (No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC), opinion and order on sanctions, June 22, 2023, ECF No. 54), slip op. at 7–9, 15–17 (Findings of Fact ¶¶ 13–14, 18, 22, 36, 38–40). The filing was an affirmation in opposition to a motion to dismiss; the court’s orders of April 11 and 12 required copies of the cited decisions; the April 25 affidavit annexed excerpts only; the respondents acknowledged that the decisions were generated by ChatGPT, and the court found that Schwartz had no full text of any of them and quoted only from chatbot excerpts. The inference in the sentence that follows is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-diaballein]: Henry George Liddell and Robert Scott, *A Greek-English Lexicon*, rev. Henry Stuart Jones with Roderick McKenzie, 9th ed. (Clarendon Press, 1940), s.vv. “συμβάλλω” (“throw together,” “bring together”), “διαβάλλω” (“throw or carry over or across”; “set at variance”; “attack a man’s character, calumniate”; also “accuse”) and “διάβολος” (“slanderer”; “enemy,” Septuagint Esther 7.4, 8.1; “Satan,” 1 Chronicles 21.1 in the Septuagint; “the Devil,” Matthew 4.1). “Throwing apart” is not a gloss the lexicon gives; it is the author’s reading of the prefix.

[^s01-m03-s01-spencerbrown]: G. Spencer-Brown, *Laws of Form* (Allen & Unwin, 1969), chap. 11, “Equations of the second degree,” 57–58, where an expression that re-enters itself is given an imaginary state, a state of time rather than of space. Reading the hardened opposition as this alternation arrested is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-monocultures]: The analysis of the two monocultures is the author’s. Its application to party politics illustrates the structure and makes no empirical claim about any particular electorate.

[^s01-m03-s01-lacan-nof]: Jacques Lacan, “On a Question Prior to Any Possible Treatment of Psychosis” (1957–58), in Lacan, *Écrits*, 445–88; and Lacan, *Psychoses*. The account of the parent as administering an order that binds them to obligations toward the child is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-wolin]: Sheldon S. Wolin, *Democracy Incorporated: Managed Democracy and the Specter of Inverted Totalitarianism* (Princeton University Press, 2008), chap. 3 (“Totalitarianism’s Inversion, Democracy’s Perversion”), chap. 8 (“The Politics of Superpower: Managed Democracy”) and chap. 11 (“Inverted Totalitarianism: Antecedents and Precedents”). The representative as the face of that power, and the reading of the representative as scapegoat that follows, with its two collapses, are the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-john]: John 12:31 (see also 14:30, 16:11), “the prince of this world”; 18:36; on the Comforter (Greek *paraklētos*), 14:16, 26; compare 17:21 (King James Version, eBible `eng-kjv2006`, standardized 1769 text). The reading of Father, Son and Spirit through `0/1` is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-hamartia]: Liddell and Scott, *Greek-English Lexicon*, s.vv. “ἁμαρτία” (“a failure, fault”; “error of judgement,” Thucydides 1.32; in philosophy and religion “guilt, sin,” Plato, *Laws* 660c; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* 1148a3; Septuagint Genesis 18.20; John 8.46) and “ἁμαρτάνω” (“miss the mark,” first of a thrown spear, *Iliad* 5.287, then “do wrong, err, sin”). The sense “miss the mark” belongs first to the verb. The reading of the missed mark through the symbolon is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-native]: The definition is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-theodicy]: G. W. Leibniz, *Essais de Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l’homme et l’origine du mal* (Amsterdam: Isaac Troyel, 1710); in English, *Theodicy: Essays on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man, and the Origin of Evil*, trans. E. M. Huggard, ed. Austin Farrer (Open Court, 1985). Leibniz formed the word from *theos*, god, and *dikē*, justice, and had used it in French and Latin forms in the mid-1690s; see Thomas Feeney, “Leibniz on the Problem of Evil,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, first published January 12, 2026.

[^s01-m03-s01-omni]: The completion of the four classical predicates by omnivalence and omni-lemmicity is the author’s. On *lēmma*, from *lambanein*, see Liddell and Scott, *Greek-English Lexicon*, s.v. “λῆμμα”: “anything received,” and in logic a “statement taken as true,” an assumption, especially a premiss (Aristotle, *Topics* 101a14, 156a21).

[^s01-m03-s01-nirguna]: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6 (“No, no!” in Max Müller’s rendering, not “not this, not this”); see also 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15, in *The Upanishads, Part II*, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15 (Clarendon Press, 1884), 108. For Eckhart’s distinction between God and Godhead, see his German sermon 52, “Beati pauperes spiritu” (Josef Quint’s number), in *The Complete Mystical Works of Meister Eckhart*, trans. and ed. Maurice O’C. Walshe, rev. Bernard McGinn (Crossroad, 2009).

[^s01-m03-s01-exodus]: Exod. 3:12, 14 (JPS 1917, in the Mechon Mamre Hebrew–English text): “Certainly I will be with thee”; “I AM THAT I AM.” The Hebrew *ehyeh asher ehyeh* also admits the rendering “I will be what I will be”: the note to Exod. 3:14 in the 1985 JPS *Tanakh* calls the meaning of the Hebrew uncertain and lists “I Am That I Am,” “I Am Who I Am” and “I Will Be What I Will Be” among the renderings.

[^s01-m03-s01-aion-shadow]: C. G. Jung, *Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 9, pt. 2 (Princeton University Press, 1979), ¶14 for the first two quoted phrases (the shadow as a moral problem; recognizing its dark aspects as present and real) and ¶16 for the third (projection placing the cause of the emotion in the other person).

[^s01-m03-s01-kelo]: *Kelo v. City of New London*, 545 U.S. 469 (2005). Facts: 472–75 (the New London Development Corporation, “a private nonprofit entity,” 473; Pfizer’s adjacent research facility, 473; the plan’s hotel, about 80 residences and office parcels, 474; the city council’s approval in January 2000 and its authorisation of the corporation to acquire property by eminent domain in the city’s name, 475). Holding: the plan serves a “public use,” 483–84 and 489–90. Justice Stevens wrote for the Court, joined by Justices Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; Justice O’Connor dissented, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas, *id.* at 494; Justice Thomas also dissented, *id.* at 505.

[^s01-m03-s01-pfizer]: Patrick McGeehan, “Pfizer to Leave City That Won Land-Use Case,” *New York Times*, November 12, 2009, https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/13/nyregion/13pfizer.html (print headline “… Land-Use Suit,” New York edition, p. A1). Pfizer announced on Monday, November 9, that it would leave New London; the article describes the cleared land on which the planned hotel, stores and condominiums were never built. For the long vacancy: JC Sevcik, “9 Years after SCOTUS’ *Kelo* Ruling, Houses Seized under Eminent Domain Remain Undeveloped,” UPI, March 20, 2014; John Penney, “Construction of 500 Apartments at Fort Trumbull Still a Go,” *The Day* (New London, CT), July 17, 2024 (parcels vacant for almost twenty years). The text states both facts generally and claims no figures.

[^s01-m03-s01-slapp]: George W. Pring and Penelope Canan, *SLAPPs: Getting Sued for Speaking Out* (Temple University Press, 1996), chap. 1 (definition and process). Pring and Canan coined the term; their earlier article is Penelope Canan and George W. Pring, “Strategic Lawsuits against Public Participation,” *Social Problems* 35, no. 5 (1988): 506–19, https://doi.org/10.1525/sp.1988.35.5.03a00030. For reputation-management firms and wealthy claimants, see, for example, United Kingdom, Ministry of Justice, *Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs): A Call for Evidence* (2022), 3, 5. The compression of the suit’s aim as burdening critics more than winning is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-carlin]: George Carlin, *Life Is Worth Losing*, directed by Rocco Urbisci (HBO, broadcast live November 5, 2005, from the Beacon Theatre, New York), in the closing routine on “the real owners” of the country, shortly before the “American dream” line. The locator is the routine; the wording is checked against an unofficial transcript only. The reading of the line as syn-ballein for members and dia-ballein for outsiders is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-dialog]: Dell Cameron and Yulia Almazova, “Leak Exposes Members of Peter Thiel’s Secretive ‘Dialog’ Society,” *Wired*, June 16, 2026, https://www.wired.com/story/leak-exposes-members-of-peter-thiels-secretive-dialog-society/; Dell Cameron, Dhruv Mehrotra, and Yulia Almazova, “How the Peter Thiel-Linked Dialog Club Secretly Ranks Its Members,” *Wired*, June 18, 2026, https://www.wired.com/story/how-peter-thiels-private-dialog-club-secretly-ranks-its-members/. The first article reports a website directory of 113 names (independently verified by *Wired*; it lists two US senators and sitting administration officials, among them the Treasury secretary) and a separate registration list for the August 2026 retreat naming 222 people (it lists a NATO commander among others); the second gives the 2006 founding by Thiel and Auren Hoffman and reports the grades by wealth and fame, the relationship tracking and the algorithmic matching of whom attendees meet and sit with. *Wired* itself says the registration records “appear to show” who attends, and the retreat had not yet taken place; inclusion in the directory or the registration records, active membership and attendance are different things, so the text names offices and sectors and calls no individual a member. The reading of the leak as a topology is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-epstein-redaction]: Epstein Files Transparency Act, Pub. L. No. 119-38, § 2(b)(1), (c), 139 Stat. 656, 657 (2025) (no record to be redacted “on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity”); Todd Blanche to Members of Congress, December 19, 2025, letter on the production of the Epstein files, U.S. Department of Justice, 1–4, https://www.justice.gov/opa/media/1434851/dl (six pages). The letter gives the Review Protocol’s five grounds of redaction and a “limited amount” of privileged withholding (2) and the victim-name redactions and the numbering of the released records (3); it does not quantify the redactions. On their extent: CBS News counted at least 550 pages entirely redacted in the first release (Joe Walsh, “Over 500 Pages in Initial Epstein Files Release Were Entirely Blacked Out, CBS News Finds,” *CBS News*, December 20, 2025, updated December 21, 2025, https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/epstein-files-redaction-over-500-pages-entirely-blacked-out); the Department reported about 3.5 million pages published by January 30, 2026 and gave no count of redactions (U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, “Department of Justice Publishes 3.5 Million Responsive Pages in Compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act,” press release, January 30, 2026, https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/department-justice-publishes-35-million-responsive-pages-compliance-epstein-files); and Representatives Massie and Khanna, having viewed the unredacted files, said the names of six men had been redacted, which the Department answered by pointing to legal requirements (Yashraj Sharma, “Six Men Named in US Congress: Why Is So Much Redacted in the Epstein Files?,” *Al Jazeera*, February 11, 2026, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/11/six-men-named-in-us-congress-why-is-so-much-redacted-in-the-epstein-files). The record shows extensive and contested redaction, not total redaction; the characterisation of it as an instance of obfuscation is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-snowden-assange]: Edward Snowden: criminal complaint filed in the Eastern District of Virginia and made public on June 21, 2013, charging theft of government property and Espionage Act offences (Will Dunham, “Federal Prosecutors Charge Edward Snowden over NSA Leaks,” Reuters, June 21, 2013, reproduced in *Christian Science Monitor*, https://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/amphtml/USA/2013/0621/Federal-prosecutors-charge-Edward-Snowden-over-NSA-leaks); temporary asylum in Russia from August 1, 2013 (“Snowden Leaves Moscow Airport,” *Al Jazeera*, August 1, 2013, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2013/8/1/snowden-leaves-moscow-airport); he has lived in Russia since. Julian Assange: arrested in London on April 11, 2019 on a US extradition request; an eighteen-count superseding indictment in the Eastern District of Virginia, seventeen counts under the Espionage Act provisions of 18 U.S.C. § 793, was filed May 23, 2019 (Superseding Indictment, *United States v. Assange*, No. 1:18-cr-00111-CMH, ECF No. 31 (E.D. Va. filed May 23, 2019), 1, https://www.justice.gov/d9/press-releases/attachments/2019/05/23/assange_superseding_indictment_1.pdf); held in Belmarsh Prison from about April 11, 2019 pending extradition, about sixty-two months, until the plea agreement of June 2024, under which he pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands to one count of conspiracy to obtain and disclose national defense information, was sentenced to time served and returned to Australia (Plea Agreement, *United States v. Assange*, No. CR 24-00014 (D.N. Mar. I. June 2024), 12, https://justice.gov/opa/media/1358636/dl). The comparison of the two cases is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-digit]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.vv. “digitus” (“a finger”; *computare digitis*, “to count on the fingers”) and “manipulus” (“a handful, a bundle,” formed from *manus* and the root of *plenus*). Harper, *Online Etymology Dictionary*, s.v. “digit,” dates *digit* as a numeral below ten to the late fourteenth century, numerals under ten having been counted on the fingers. *Manipulation*, attested by 1730 of a method of digging ore, reached English through French; *The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language*, 5th ed., s.v. “manipulation,” adds a Spanish stage, and Harper, s.v. “manipulation,” gives French *manipule*, “handful,” a pharmacists’ measure.

[^s01-m03-s01-nietzsche-market]: Friedrich Nietzsche, *The Gay Science: With a Prelude in Rhymes and an Appendix of Songs*, trans. Walter Kaufmann (New York: Vintage Books, 1974), §125 (“The Madman”), 181–82. In the parable the madman lights a lantern in the morning and runs to the marketplace (*Markt*) to announce that God is dead. The reading of why the news belongs there is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-trust]: The distinctions among trust, knowledge, belief and faith, and the account of faith as lucid continuation through the limit, are the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-fides]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.v. “fides”: “trust in a person or thing, faith, confidence, reliance, credence, belief,” with the sense of credibility illustrated from Cicero, *De officiis* 2.9.33 (“to give confidence”), and *Pro Sulla* 3.10 (testimony); the entry derives *fides* from *fido*.

[^s01-m03-s01-arbiter]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.vv. “arbiter” (first “a spectator, beholder, hearer, an eye-witness, a witness,” then the judicial sense of one appointed to inquire into a cause and settle it) and “arbitror.” The second entry gives the construction *fidem alicui arbitrari*, “to adjudge, i.e. to give, credit to one,” citing Plautus, *Bacchides* 3.6.41. The line, collated in Friedrich Leo’s text (*Plauti Comoediae*, vol. 1 [Weidmann, 1895], line 570), reads *Postremo, si pergis parvam mihi fidem arbitrarier*, so the lexicon’s formula is a lemmatised form of the attested phrase.

[^s01-m03-s01-arbitration]: The analysis of criterion, delineation and arbitration, and the sentence on arbitration and tacit trust, are the author’s.

#### #3 · The Formal-Limit Genealogy

[^s01-m04-s01-principia]: Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell, *Principia Mathematica*, 3 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1910–13), vol. 1, preface, pp. v–viii (the 1910 preface, reprinted in the 2nd ed. of 1925, from which the pages are given). The aim and method of the work: v–vi. The chief reason for accepting any theory of the principles of mathematics being inductive, in that it enables us to deduce ordinary mathematics: v. The months of work needed to show a hypothesis untenable, the conclusion that some form of the doctrine of types must be adopted, and the particular form advocated not being logically indispensable, so that little of the book would change with another: vii. The symbolism developed in practice and in large part new because the ideas had not been symbolised before: vii–viii.

[^s01-m04-s01-russell-faith]: Bertrand Russell, “Reflections on My Eightieth Birthday,” in *Portraits from Memory and Other Essays* (Simon and Schuster, 1956), 54; the sentence on “some twenty years of very arduous toil” and the conclusion that nothing more could be done to make mathematical knowledge indubitable follows at 55. Pages are those of the American edition; the British edition (Allen & Unwin, 1956) is paginated differently.

[^s01-m04-s01-frege]: Gottlob Frege, *Grundgesetze der Arithmetik, begriffsschriftlich abgeleitet*, 2 vols. (Hermann Pohle, 1893–1903), 1:36 (§20), Basic Law V, which states that the value-range of one function coincides with that of another just when the two functions agree at every argument. The essay’s paraphrase, that any clearly stated condition gathers a collection, is the form of the principle that Russell’s argument uses. Bertrand Russell to Gottlob Frege, June 16, 1902, and Frege to Russell, June 22, 1902, in *From Frege to Gödel: A Source Book in Mathematical Logic, 1879–1931*, ed. Jean van Heijenoort (Harvard University Press, 1967), 124–25 and 127–28. Frege’s appendix to vol. 2, headed “Nachwort” and dated October 1902, *Grundgesetze*, 2:253–65. On the failure of Frege’s attempted repair and his later papers, see Edward N. Zalta, “Gottlob Frege,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege/. The library-catalogue illustration is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-russell]: Bertrand Russell, “Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types,” *American Journal of Mathematics* 30, no. 3 (1908): 237, §IV, “The Hierarchy of Types,” https://doi.org/10.2307/2369948. The theory is carried into Whitehead and Russell, *Principia Mathematica*, vol. 1, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1925), introduction, chap. 2, “The Theory of Logical Types,” 37 ff.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-concreteness]: Alfred North Whitehead, *Science and the Modern World* (Macmillan, 1925), chap. 3, “The Century of Genius,” 74–75, where the error of mistaking the abstract for the concrete is first named the “Fallacy of Misplaced Concreteness”; see also 82 and, at the head of chap. 4, 85.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-smw]: Whitehead, *Science and the Modern World*, chap. 12, “Religion and Science,” 267 (the contradiction sentence).
